claim: The HD_CFD library consists of more than 2600 plasmids and 1700 fly lines.
source: The library consists currently of more than 2600 plasmids and 1700 fly lines with a focus on targeting kinases, phosphatases and transcription factors, each expressing two sgRNAs under control of the Gal4/UAS system.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract with specific numbers.

claim: The HD_CFD library focuses on targeting kinases, phosphatases and transcription factors.
source: The library consists currently of more than 2600 plasmids and 1700 fly lines with a focus on targeting kinases, phosphatases and transcription factors, each expressing two sgRNAs under control of the Gal4/UAS system.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract.

claim: Each HD_CFD line expresses two sgRNAs under control of the Gal4/UAS system.
source: The library consists currently of more than 2600 plasmids and 1700 fly lines with a focus on targeting kinases, phosphatases and transcription factors, each expressing two sgRNAs under control of the Gal4/UAS system.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract.

claim: Conditional CRISPR mutagenesis is robust across many target genes.
source: We show that conditional CRISPR mutagenesis is robust across many target genes and can be efficiently employed in various somatic tissues, as well as the germline.
evidence: Demonstrated through multiple experimental validations across different genes and tissues.

claim: Conditional CRISPR mutagenesis can be efficiently employed in various somatic tissues and the germline.
source: We show that conditional CRISPR mutagenesis is robust across many target genes and can be efficiently employed in various somatic tissues, as well as the germline.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments in wing discs, midgut, and germline.

claim: Excessive amounts of Cas9 protein cause artefacts.
source: In order to prevent artefacts commonly associated with excessive amounts of Cas9 protein, we have developed a series of novel UAS-Cas9 transgenes, which allow fine tuning of Cas9 expression to achieve high gene editing activity without detectable toxicity.
evidence: Stated as a known problem that motivated the development of tunable Cas9 transgenes.

claim: The UAS-uCas9 series allows fine tuning of Cas9 expression to achieve high gene editing activity without detectable toxicity.
source: In order to prevent artefacts commonly associated with excessive amounts of Cas9 protein, we have developed a series of novel UAS-Cas9 transgenes, which allow fine tuning of Cas9 expression to achieve high gene editing activity without detectable toxicity.
evidence: Demonstrated through systematic characterization of the UAS-uCas9 series.

claim: The vast majority of transgenic sgRNA lines mediate efficient gene disruption.
source: Functional assays, as well as direct sequencing of genomic sgRNA target sites, indicates that the vast majority of transgenic sgRNA lines mediate efficient gene disruption.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data and functional assays.

claim: The study conducted the largest fully transgenic CRISPR screen in any metazoan organism.
source: Furthermore, we conducted the so far largest fully transgenic CRISPR screen in any metazoan organism, which further supported the high efficiency and accuracy of our library and revealed many so far uncharacterized genes essential for development.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract.

claim: The CRISPR screen revealed many uncharacterized genes essential for development.
source: Furthermore, we conducted the so far largest fully transgenic CRISPR screen in any metazoan organism, which further supported the high efficiency and accuracy of our library and revealed many so far uncharacterized genes essential for development.
evidence: Supported by the lethality screen results.

claim: RNAi is often limited by incomplete penetrance due to residual gene expression.
source: However, RNAi is often limited by incomplete penetrance due to residual gene expression and can suffer from off-target effects (Echeverri et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2006; Perkins et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RNAi can suffer from off-target effects.
source: However, RNAi is often limited by incomplete penetrance due to residual gene expression and can suffer from off-target effects (Echeverri et al., 2006; Ma et al., 2006; Perkins et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In Drosophila only 20% of genes have associated mutant alleles.
source: For example, in Drosophila only 20% of genes have associated mutant alleles (Kaufman, 2017).
evidence: Cited from Kaufman, 2017.

claim: Not all Cas9-mediated indel mutations abrogate gene function.
source: However, not all Cas9-mediated indel mutations abrogate gene function.
evidence: Stated as a known limitation of CRISPR mutagenesis.

claim: Several sgRNAs are often required to generate bi-allelic loss-of-function mutations in all cells.
source: The efficiency of such multiplexing strategies has been demonstrated in flies, mice, fish and plants, and several sgRNAs are often required to generate bi-allelic loss-of function mutations in all cells (Port and Bullock, 2016; Xie et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cas9 expression vectors with tissue-specific enhancers often display 'leaky' Cas9 expression in other tissues.
source: However, Cas9 expression vectors with tissue-specific enhancers often display 'leaky' Cas9 expression in other tissues and poor control of CRISPR mutagenesis has been observed in multiple systems, including flies, mice and patient derived xenografts (Chen et al., 2017; Dow et al., 2015; Hulton et al., 2019; Port and Bullock, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Expressing both Cas9 and sgRNA from conditional regulatory elements can result in tightly controlled genome editing.
source: It has recently been demonstrated that expressing both Cas9 and sgRNA from conditional regulatory elements can result in tightly controlled genome editing (Port and Bullock, 2016), but the robustness of such a strategy across many genomic target sites has so far not been explored.
evidence: Cited from Port and Bullock, 2016.

claim: Conditional expression of both Cas9 and sgRNAs is necessary to achieve tight control of mutagenesis.
source: We have previously shown that conditional expression of both Cas9 and sgRNAs is necessary to achieve tight control of mutagenesis (Figure 1B; Port and Bullock, 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous work by the authors.

claim: pCFD6-arm2x results in loss of Arm protein exclusively in the Gal4 expression domain in nearly all cells.
source: Gene editing with pCFD6-arm2x results in loss of Arm protein exclusively in the Gal4 expression domain in nearly all cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry in Figure 1C.

claim: CRISPR mutagenesis of Notch in intestinal stem cells drives tumor formation in the midgut.
source: Conditional CRISPR mutagenesis of Notch in intestinal stem cells drives tumor formation in the midgut.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1D.

claim: Notch mutagenesis by CRISPR induces strong overgrowth in both male and female midguts.
source: Interestingly, we observed a qualitative difference between perturbation of N expression by RNAi, which only induces hyperplasia in female flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Hudry et al., 2016; Siudeja et al., 2015), and N mutagenesis by CRISPR, which induces strong overgrowth in both male and female midguts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data comparing RNAi and CRISPR approaches.

claim: Notch RNAi only induces hyperplasia in female flies.
source: Interestingly, we observed a qualitative difference between perturbation of N expression by RNAi, which only induces hyperplasia in female flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Hudry et al., 2016; Siudeja et al., 2015), and N mutagenesis by CRISPR, which induces strong overgrowth in both male and female midguts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: nos-Gal4VP16 UAS-Cas9.P1 pCFD6-sgRNA2x flies were viable and morphologically normal, demonstrating tightly restricted mutagenesis.
source: Despite the fact that all five genes are essential for Drosophila development and act in multiple tissues, nos-Gal4VP16 UAS-Cas9.P1 pCFD6-sgRNA2x flies were viable and morphologically normal, demonstrating tightly restricted mutagenesis.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental observation of fly viability.

claim: Crosses with pCFD6-sgRNA2x targeting neur, N, ct and Ras85D passed on mutations to most or all analysed offspring.
source: Crosses with pCFD6-sgRNA2x targeting neur, N, ct and Ras85D passed on mutations to most or all analysed offspring (Figure 1G).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data in Figure 1G.

claim: Mutations were often found on both target sites, were frequently out-of-frame and included large deletions of 8 and 14 kb between the sgRNA target sites.
source: Mutations were often found on both target sites, were frequently out-of-frame and included large deletions of 8 and 14 kb between the sgRNA target sites (Figure 1G).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data in Figure 1G.

claim: nos-Gal4VP16 UAS-Cas9.P1 pCFD6-dpp2x flies produced only few viable offspring of which only 1/11 carried a mutation, which was in-frame.
source: In contrast, nos-Gal4VP16 UAS-Cas9.P1 pCFD6-dpp2x flies produced only few viable offspring of which only 1/11 carried a mutation, which was in-frame.
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data.

claim: dpp is haploinsufficient.
source: Since dpp is known to be haploinsufficient (St Johnston et al., 1990), this is consistent with a high number of dpp loss-of function alleles being transmitted to the next generation.
evidence: Cited from St Johnston et al., 1990.

claim: Expression of high amounts of Cas9 protein is toxic in various organisms.
source: We and others have shown that expression of high amounts of Cas9 protein is toxic in various organisms (Jiang et al., 2014; Poe et al., 2019; Port et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Overexpression of Cas9 in the wing imaginal disc of nub-Gal4 UAS-cas9.P2 animals results in a strong induction of apoptosis.
source: For example, overexpression of Cas9 in the wing imaginal disc of nub-Gal4 UAS-cas9.P2 animals results in a strong induction of apoptosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only relatively low levels of Cas9 are sufficient for efficient gene editing.
source: Since only relatively low levels of Cas9 are sufficient for efficient gene editing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), we sought to engineer a system that would allow to tune Cas9 expression to optimally balance activity and toxicity.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The UAS-uCas9 series uses upstream open reading frames (uORF) of different length to predictably reduce translation of the main, downstream ORF.
source: We employed a method that uses upstream open reading frames (uORF) of different length to predictably reduce translation of the main, downstream ORF (Ferreira et al., 2013; Kozak, 2001; Southall et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: The UAS-uCas9 plasmids resulted in Cas9 protein levels inversely correlated with the length of the uORF.
source: When combined with nos-cas9 these plasmids resulted in Cas9 protein levels inversely correlated with the length of the uORF (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2B.

claim: Reducing the amount of Cas9 protein resulted in a strong decrease in the number of apoptotic cells.
source: Reducing the amount of Cas9 protein resulted in a strong decrease in the number of apoptotic cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2C.

claim: Three UAS-uCas9 transgenes with moderate levels of Cas9 expression and apoptosis levels similar to controls did mediate full on-target gene editing activity at the evi locus in wing imaginal discs.
source: Importantly, three UAS-uCas9 transgenes with moderate levels of Cas9 expression and apoptosis levels similar to controls did mediate full on-target gene editing activity at the evi locus in wing imaginal discs (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2D.

claim: Some Gal4 UAS-uMCas9 lines resulted in mutagenesis exclusively in cells positive for Cas9 at that stage.
source: We found that while some Gal4 UAS-uMCas9 lines resulted in mutagenesis exclusively in cells positive for Cas9 at that stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E), others had much broader mutagenesis patterns (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in figures.

claim: ptc-Gal4 is expressed in a narrow band of cells along the anterior-posterior boundary in third instar wing discs.
source: For example, in third instar wing discs ptc-Gal4 is expressed in a narrow band of cells along the anterior-posterior boundary (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2E.

claim: CRISPR mutagenesis with ptc-Gal4 frequently leads to mutations throughout the entire anterior compartment.
source: However, CRISPR mutagenesis with ptc-Gal4 frequently leads to mutations throughout the entire anterior compartment (Figure 2E'), likely reflecting broader expression of ptc-Gal4 in early development or expression at low level in this domain.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2E'.

claim: Gal80ts mediated strong inhibition of mutagenesis in ptc-Gal4 UAS-uMCas9 tub-Gal80ts flies at the restrictive temperature of 18°C.
source: While Gal80ts mediated strong inhibition of mutagenesis in ptc-Gal4 UAS-uMCas9 tub-Gal80ts flies at the restrictive temperature of 18°C, we still observed mutagenesis in Gal4-expressing cells in 11/24 wing discs, indicating residual Gal4 activity (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2F.

claim: Mutagenesis was still observed at 18°C in 11/24 discs in ptc-Gal4 UAS-uMCas9 tub-Gal80ts flies, indicating incomplete Gal4 suppression by Gal80ts.
source: While Gal80ts mediated strong inhibition of mutagenesis in ptc-Gal4 UAS-uMCas9 tub-Gal80ts flies at the restrictive temperature of 18°C, we still observed mutagenesis in Gal4-expressing cells in 11/24 wing discs, indicating residual Gal4 activity (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2F.

claim: A brief pulse of Flp recombinase can be used to excise the GFP cassette at the desired time and induce Cas9 expression.
source: A brief pulse of Flp recombinase (from a hs-Flp transgene) can be used to excise the GFP cassette at the desired time and induce Cas9 expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental validation.

claim: Loss of Ct protein was observed exclusively in cells that had lost GFP expression.
source: We validated this approach by mutagenizing ct in a negatively marked subset of cells in the wing disc and observed loss of Ct protein exclusively in cells that had lost GFP expression (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2G.

claim: The HD_CFD library currently contains 2622 plasmids and 1739 fly stocks targeting 1513 unique genes.
source: We then generated a large-scale transgenic sgRNA library, which we collectively refer to as the 'Heidelberg CRISPR Fly Design Library' (short HD_CFD library). This growing resource currently contains 2622 plasmids and 1739 fly stocks targeting 1513 unique genes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Stated directly with specific numbers.

claim: Fly lines are available for 545/754 (72%) transcription factors.
source: Fly lines are so far available for 545/754 (72%) transcription factors, 199/230 (87%) protein kinases and 141/207 (68%) phosphatases (Figure 2D).
evidence: Stated directly with specific numbers.

claim: Fly lines are available for 199/230 (87%) protein kinases.
source: Fly lines are so far available for 545/754 (72%) transcription factors, 199/230 (87%) protein kinases and 141/207 (68%) phosphatases (Figure 2D).
evidence: Stated directly with specific numbers.

claim: Fly lines are available for 141/207 (68%) phosphatases.
source: Fly lines are so far available for 545/754 (72%) transcription factors, 199/230 (87%) protein kinases and 141/207 (68%) phosphatases (Figure 2D).
evidence: Stated directly with specific numbers.

claim: The vast majority (26/28) of HD_CFD sgRNA lines resulted in gene editing on both target sites.
source: We found that the vast majority (26/28) of HD_CFD sgRNA lines resulted in gene editing on both target sites (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data in Figure 4A.

claim: For 12/28 of lines editing on both sites was inferred to be at least 50%.
source: For 12/28 of lines editing on both sites was inferred to be at least 50% and 23/28 reached this threshold on at least one target site.
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data and ICE analysis.

claim: 23/28 lines reached at least 50% editing on at least one target site.
source: For 12/28 of lines editing on both sites was inferred to be at least 50% and 23/28 reached this threshold on at least one target site.
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data and ICE analysis.

claim: Only a single line (HD_CFD00032) resulted in no detectable gene editing at either sgRNA target site.
source: In contrast, only a single line (HD_CFD00032) resulted in no detectable gene editing at either sgRNA target site.
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data.

claim: 290/639 (45%) of all crosses did not yield any viable offspring.
source: 290/639 (45%) of all crosses did not yield any viable offspring, while 269 (42%) lines produced viable adults and 53 (8%) of the lines resulted in lethality with incomplete penetrance (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by the lethality screen data.

claim: 269 (42%) lines produced viable adults.
source: 290/639 (45%) of all crosses did not yield any viable offspring, while 269 (42%) lines produced viable adults and 53 (8%) of the lines resulted in lethality with incomplete penetrance (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by the lethality screen data.

claim: 53 (8%) of the lines resulted in lethality with incomplete penetrance.
source: 290/639 (45%) of all crosses did not yield any viable offspring, while 269 (42%) lines produced viable adults and 53 (8%) of the lines resulted in lethality with incomplete penetrance (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by the lethality screen data.

claim: Of 210 lines targeting known essential genes, 167 (79%) resulted in lethality.
source: This resulted in a list of 210 lines that target known essential genes. Of those, 167 (79%) resulted in lethality, 20 (10%) were scored as semi-lethal, and 23 (11%) gave rise to viable adult offspring.
evidence: Demonstrated by the lethality screen data.

claim: Of 210 lines targeting known essential genes, 20 (10%) were scored as semi-lethal.
source: This resulted in a list of 210 lines that target known essential genes. Of those, 167 (79%) resulted in lethality, 20 (10%) were scored as semi-lethal, and 23 (11%) gave rise to viable adult offspring.
evidence: Demonstrated by the lethality screen data.

claim: Of 210 lines targeting known essential genes, 23 (11%) gave rise to viable adult offspring.
source: This resulted in a list of 210 lines that target known essential genes. Of those, 167 (79%) resulted in lethality, 20 (10%) were scored as semi-lethal, and 23 (11%) gave rise to viable adult offspring.
evidence: Demonstrated by the lethality screen data.

claim: Among the targets of sgRNA lines that produced false-negative results there was a strong enrichment of genes known to play important roles, and to be highly expressed, during early embryonic development.
source: Interestingly, among the targets of sgRNA lines that produced false-negative results there was a strong enrichment of genes known to play important roles, and to be highly expressed, during early embryonic development.
evidence: Inferred from expression data analysis.

claim: Sequencing the sgRNA target sites in randomly selected false-negative lines revealed efficient gene editing on one or both sites in 3/3 lines.
source: Furthermore, sequencing the sgRNA target sites in randomly selected false-negative lines revealed efficient gene editing on one or both sites in 3/3 lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that false-negative results often arise due to mRNA perdurance, not inactive sgRNAs.
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: False-negative results often arise due to mRNA perdurance, not inactive sgRNAs.
source: Furthermore, sequencing the sgRNA target sites in randomly selected false-negative lines revealed efficient gene editing on one or both sites in 3/3 lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that false-negative results often arise due to mRNA perdurance, not inactive sgRNAs.
evidence: Inferred from sequencing data showing efficient editing in false-negative lines.

claim: Among 54 lines targeting genes annotated as viable, 48 (89%) gave rise to viable adult offspring.
source: Among the 639 lines present in our screen, 54 target genes are currently annotated as viable. Of those, 48 (89%) gave rise to viable adult offspring, one resulted in semi-lethal offspring and 5 (9%) produced no viable offspring.
evidence: Demonstrated by the lethality screen data.

claim: Among 54 lines targeting genes annotated as viable, one resulted in semi-lethal offspring.
source: Among the 639 lines present in our screen, 54 target genes are currently annotated as viable. Of those, 48 (89%) gave rise to viable adult offspring, one resulted in semi-lethal offspring and 5 (9%) produced no viable offspring.
evidence: Demonstrated by the lethality screen data.

claim: Among 54 lines targeting genes annotated as viable, 5 (9%) produced no viable offspring.
source: Among the 639 lines present in our screen, 54 target genes are currently annotated as viable. Of those, 48 (89%) gave rise to viable adult offspring, one resulted in semi-lethal offspring and 5 (9%) produced no viable offspring.
evidence: Demonstrated by the lethality screen data.

claim: Two of the five lines giving rise to false-positive results target the same gene (Blos1).
source: Of the five lines giving rise to false-positive results in our screen two target the same gene (Blos1), arguing against sgRNA-mediated off-target mutagenesis in this case.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: sgRNA line HD_CFD558 targets CG9890, an evolutionary conserved zinc finger protein of unknown function.
source: For example, sgRNA line HD_CFD558 targets CG9890, an evolutionary conserved (55% amino acid similarity to the human ortholog) zinc finger protein of unknown function.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: CG9890 has 55% amino acid similarity to the human ortholog.
source: For example, sgRNA line HD_CFD558 targets CG9890, an evolutionary conserved (55% amino acid similarity to the human ortholog) zinc finger protein of unknown function.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: CG6470 is targeted by HD_CFD557 and HD_CFD599 with independent sgRNAs.
source: Another interesting example is CG6470, which is targeted by HD_CFD557 and HD_CFD599 with independent sgRNAs.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: CG6470 encodes an uncharacterized zinc finger protein that is evolutionary restricted to the genus Drosophila.
source: CG6470 encodes an uncharacterized zinc finger protein that despite its essential role during development is evolutionary restricted to the genus Drosophila.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: All lines targeting genes associated with dpp/TGFb signalling resulted in offspring that had wings of abnormal size and morphology.
source: Moreover, all lines resulted in offspring that had wings of abnormal size and morphology and faithfully recapitulated the known phenotypes of loss-of function mutations of their target genes (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4E.

claim: The lines faithfully recapitulated the known phenotypes of loss-of-function mutations of their target genes.
source: Moreover, all lines resulted in offspring that had wings of abnormal size and morphology and faithfully recapitulated the known phenotypes of loss-of function mutations of their target genes (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4E.

claim: CRISPR mutagenesis in vivo can cause phenotypes that are significantly more penetrant than RNAi.
source: In support of this notion three recent studies demonstrate that CRISPR mutagenesis in vivo can cause phenotypes that are significantly more penetrant than RNAi (Meltzer et al., 2019) or are missed altogether in RNAi experiments (Delventhal et al., 2019; Schlichting et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from recent studies.

claim: CRISPR mutagenesis can reveal phenotypes that are missed altogether in RNAi experiments.
source: In support of this notion three recent studies demonstrate that CRISPR mutagenesis in vivo can cause phenotypes that are significantly more penetrant than RNAi (Meltzer et al., 2019) or are missed altogether in RNAi experiments (Delventhal et al., 2019; Schlichting et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from recent studies.

claim: The fraction of HD_CFD lines that produce no or only insufficient on-target mutations is less than 10%.
source: Furthermore, our molecular analysis of mutations induced by the CRISPR library described here, as well as the phenotypes arising from them, suggest that the fraction of lines that produce no or only insufficient on-target mutations is less than 10%, which compares favorably to current Drosophila RNAi libraries.
evidence: Inferred from sequencing and phenotypic data.

claim: CRISPR with transgenic components is effective in postmitotic neurons.
source: Furthermore, others have shown that CRISPR with transgenic components is also effective in postmitotic neurons (Delventhal et al., 2019) or in cells of the prothoracic gland, which are endoreplicating and contain multiple copies of the genome (Huynh et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Delventhal et al., 2019.

claim: CRISPR with transgenic components is effective in cells of the prothoracic gland, which are endoreplicating and contain multiple copies of the genome.
source: Furthermore, others have shown that CRISPR with transgenic components is also effective in postmitotic neurons (Delventhal et al., 2019) or in cells of the prothoracic gland, which are endoreplicating and contain multiple copies of the genome (Huynh et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Huynh et al., 2018.

claim: Sequencing of PCR amplicons generated from genomic DNA of entire flies frequently indicates mutations in over 90% of the amplicons.
source: In addition, our finding that sequencing of PCR amplicons generated from genomic DNA of entire flies frequently indicates mutations in over 90% of the amplicons suggests that CRISPR is effective in most cells of the animal.
evidence: Demonstrated by sequencing data.

claim: CRISPR is effective in most cells of the animal.
source: In addition, our finding that sequencing of PCR amplicons generated from genomic DNA of entire flies frequently indicates mutations in over 90% of the amplicons suggests that CRISPR is effective in most cells of the animal.
evidence: Inferred from sequencing data showing high mutation rates.

claim: The National Institute of Genetics (NIG) in Japan, the Transgenic RNAi Project (TRIP) at Harvard University and the Schuldiner group at the Weizmann Institute are generating collections of transgenic sgRNA lines.
source: In parallel to the CRISPR library described here, the National Institute of Genetics (NIG) in Japan, the Transgenic RNAi Project (TRIP) at Harvard University and the Schuldiner group at the Weizmann Institute are generating collections of transgenic sgRNA lines (Meltzer et al., 2019; Zirin et al., 2020; https://shigen.nig.ac.jp/fly/nigfly/).
evidence: Cited from other studies and resources.

claim: The NIG and the majority of TRIP and Weizmann libraries encode a single sgRNA per transgene.
source: First, the NIG and the majority of TRIP and Weizmann libraries encode a single sgRNAs per transgene, while all HD_CFD lines encode two sgRNAs.
evidence: Stated as a comparison between different libraries.

claim: All HD_CFD lines encode two sgRNAs.
source: First, the NIG and the majority of TRIP and Weizmann libraries encode a single sgRNAs per transgene, while all HD_CFD lines encode two sgRNAs.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: Co-expression of more than one sgRNA against the same target leads to more penetrant phenotypes and reduces the number of inactive lines.
source: Co-expression of more than one sgRNA against the same target leads to more penetrant phenotypes and reduces the number of inactive lines (Port and Bullock, 2016; Xie et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: The HD_CFD sgRNAs are encoded in pCFD6 or pCFD6.FRT, which are conditional UAS vectors.
source: Second, the HD_CFD sgRNAs are encoded in pCFD6 or pCFD6.FRT, which are conditional UAS vectors, while all other libraries so far used plasmids expressing sgRNAs from ubiquitous U6 promoters.
evidence: Stated directly in the text.

claim: All other libraries so far used plasmids expressing sgRNAs from ubiquitous U6 promoters.
source: Second, the HD_CFD sgRNAs are encoded in pCFD6 or pCFD6.FRT, which are conditional UAS vectors, while all other libraries so far used plasmids expressing sgRNAs from ubiquitous U6 promoters.
evidence: Stated as a comparison between different libraries.

claim: Expression of U6-sgRNA in combination with UAS-Cas9 alone is not sufficient to efficiently restrict mutagenesis to Gal4 expressing cells.
source: We have previously shown that expression of U6-sgRNA in combination with UAS-Cas9 alone is not sufficient to efficiently restrict mutagenesis to Gal4 expressing cells and that expression of sgRNAs from a UAS vector, such as pCFD6, results in a significant improvement in spatial and temporal control (Port and Bullock, 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous work by the authors.

claim: Expression of sgRNAs from a UAS vector, such as pCFD6, results in a significant improvement in spatial and temporal control.
source: We have previously shown that expression of U6-sgRNA in combination with UAS-Cas9 alone is not sufficient to efficiently restrict mutagenesis to Gal4 expressing cells and that expression of sgRNAs from a UAS vector, such as pCFD6, results in a significant improvement in spatial and temporal control (Port and Bullock, 2016).
evidence: Cited from previous work by the authors.

claim: The use of transgenes of the UAS-uCas9 series can reduce, but not prevent, unwanted mutagenesis in combination with U6-sgRNAs.
source: The use of transgenes of the UAS-uCas9 series can reduce, but not prevent, unwanted mutagenesis in combination with U6-sgRNAs, as leaky (i.e. Gal4 independent) Cas9 expression is reduced in the presence of a uORF.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanism of uORF-mediated translational control.

claim: An advantage of U6-sgRNA vectors is the consistent high sgRNA expression.
source: An advantage of U6-sgRNA vectors is the consistent high sgRNA expression, whereas the level of sgRNAs expressed from UAS promoters depends on the strength of the Gal4 line and can become limiting with weak Gal4 drivers (Meltzer et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated as a comparison and cited from Meltzer et al., 2019.

claim: The level of sgRNAs expressed from UAS promoters depends on the strength of the Gal4 line and can become limiting with weak Gal4 drivers.
source: An advantage of U6-sgRNA vectors is the consistent high sgRNA expression, whereas the level of sgRNAs expressed from UAS promoters depends on the strength of the Gal4 line and can become limiting with weak Gal4 drivers (Meltzer et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from Meltzer et al., 2019.

claim: pCFD6.FRT can alleviate the problem of limiting sgRNA expression by allowing users to swap the UAS promoter for a U6:3 promoter.
source: Of note, pCFD6.FRT can alleviate this problem, as users can easily swap the UAS promoter for a U6:3 promoter in cases where high sgRNA expression is a higher priority than tight conditional mutagenesis.
evidence: Stated as a feature of pCFD6.FRT.

claim: The lethality screen revealed 259 putative essential genes.
source: We validate our library by conducting a fully transgenic CRISPR mutagenesis screen, to our knowledge the so far largest in any multicellular animal, which revealed 259 putative essential genes, of which 56 are poorly characterized.
evidence: Inferred from the screen results showing 290 lethal + 53 semi-lethal lines, but the text states 259 putative essential genes.

claim: Of the 259 putative essential genes revealed by the screen, 56 are poorly characterized.
source: We validate our library by conducting a fully transgenic CRISPR mutagenesis screen, to our knowledge the so far largest in any multicellular animal, which revealed 259 putative essential genes, of which 56 are poorly characterized.
evidence: Stated directly in the discussion.

claim: A significant number of transgenic RNAi lines do not mediate efficient gene knock-down.
source: However, a significant number of these lines do not mediate efficient gene knock-down and the majority reduces mRNA levels by less than 75% (Perkins et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Perkins et al., 2015.

claim: The majority of transgenic RNAi lines reduces mRNA levels by less than 75%.
source: However, a significant number of these lines do not mediate efficient gene knock-down and the majority reduces mRNA levels by less than 75% (Perkins et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Perkins et al., 2015.
